meta.titre: Permutations and Combinations: Choosing, Arranging and Counting Cases

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Additional Mathematics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A teacher in Garoua has to form a delegation for a regional quiz and wonders how many different delegations are possible. A market trader in Douala wants to know how many ways she can display her goods in a row. Both questions are about counting without listing every case. At the GCE you must tell at once whether the order matters, and then apply the correct formula without slips.

items: Multiplication of whole numbers and simplifying fractions.
A word is a row of letters, and different orders of the same letters can give different words.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### The counting principle

If one task can be done in $m$ ways and a second, independent task in $n$ ways, then "first **and** second" can be done in $m\times n$ ways. If the tasks are alternatives ("either ... **or** ..."), the numbers of ways are **added**.

### Factorials, arrangements and selections

The factorial is $n!=n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots 3\times 2\times 1$, and $0!=1$. The key question is always: **does the order matter?**

An **arrangement** (permutation) of $r$ objects taken from $n$ different objects, where order matters:

$$
{}^{n}P_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!} \tag{1}
$$

A **selection** (combination) of $r$ objects from $n$ different objects, where order does not matter:

$$
{}^{n}C_{r}=\frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!} \tag{2}
$$

There are always $r!$ times as many arrangements as selections: ${}^{n}P_{r}=r!\times{}^{n}C_{r}$. Also ${}^{n}C_{r}={}^{n}C_{n-r}$, which saves work: ${}^{10}C_{8}={}^{10}C_{2}$.

| Situation | Order matters? | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| Choose a team of 4 from 9 players | No | ${}^{9}C_{4}$ |
| Award first, second and third prizes among 9 players | Yes | ${}^{9}P_{3}$ |
| Choose 2 boys **and** 3 girls | No, for each group | multiply two combinations |

### Mixed groups

When a group must contain given numbers from different sets, choose from each set separately and **multiply**.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When some of the objects (for example letters of a word) are identical.
variantes.contenu_markdown: If $n$ objects include $p$ identical objects of one kind and $q$ of another, the number of different arrangements is $\dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!}$. For the letters of LEVEL, $L$ appears twice and $E$ appears twice, so the number is $\dfrac{5!}{2!\,2!}=\dfrac{120}{4}=30$. Dividing removes the arrangements that differ only by swapping identical letters.

variantes.nom: Conditions: at least, at most, a given person
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a selection carries a restriction.
variantes.contenu_markdown: For a given person who **must** be in the group, choose the remaining places from the other $n-1$ people. For 'at least', either add the allowed cases one by one or subtract the forbidden cases from the total: $\text{total}-\text{(none)}-\text{(exactly one)}$. Choose the shorter route and check it with the other when you can.

sections.enonce_markdown: A school choir group is made of 3 girls and 2 boys, chosen from 8 girls and 5 boys who volunteered at a school in Bafoussam. (a) In how many ways can the group be chosen? (b) From the 5 members of a chosen group, a leader and a deputy leader are named. In how many ways can this be done?

etapes.action: Decide whether order matters for the group.
etapes.justification: Choosing members of a group gives no rank to anyone, so use combinations.
The group needs girls **and** boys, so multiply.
Here the order matters (leader first, deputy second), so use arrangements of 2 from 5.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) There are **560** possible groups. (b) A leader and a deputy can be named in **20** ways.

items.erreur_markdown: Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: ${}^{8}P_{3}=336$.
items.pourquoi_faux: A committee has no ranks, so ABC and CBA are the same committee. Permutations count each committee $3!$ times.
'And' means both choices are made together, so the numbers of ways multiply. Addition is only for alternatives.
Swapping the three identical A's, or the two identical N's, gives the same word, so 720 over-counts.
This is the formula for ${}^{n}P_{r}$. It forgets to divide by $r!$ for the orderings inside the selection.
By definition $0!=1$. With $0!=0$ the fraction would involve division by zero.

items.enonce_markdown: Evaluate ${}^{8}P_{3}$ and ${}^{8}C_{3}$, and explain in one sentence why the first is larger.
items.solution_markdown: ${}^{8}P_{3}=8\times7\times6=\mathbf{336}$. ${}^{8}C_{3}=\dfrac{336}{3!}=\dfrac{336}{6}=\mathbf{56}$. Each selection of 3 people can be ordered in $3!=6$ ways, so there are 6 times more arrangements than selections.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) How many different arrangements are there of all the letters of the word BANANA? (b) How many of them begin with the letter B?
items.solution_markdown: (a) There are 6 letters with A three times and N twice: $\dfrac{6!}{3!\,2!}=\dfrac{720}{12}=\mathbf{60}$. (b) Fix B in first place; the letters AANAN remain, with A three times and N twice: $\dfrac{5!}{3!\,2!}=\dfrac{120}{12}=\mathbf{10}$.

items.enonce_markdown: A football club in Buea has 6 men and 4 women who are all willing to join a committee of 5 people. (a) How many committees contain at least 2 women? (b) How many committees of 5 include one particular man, Mr Fon?
items.solution_markdown: (a) Total committees: ${}^{10}C_{5}=252$. Committees with no woman: ${}^{6}C_{5}=6$. Committees with exactly one woman: ${}^{4}C_{1}\times{}^{6}C_{4}=4\times15=60$. So at least 2 women: $252-6-60=\mathbf{186}$. Check by cases: $\;{}^{4}C_{2}{}^{6}C_{3}+{}^{4}C_{3}{}^{6}C_{2}+{}^{4}C_{4}{}^{6}C_{1}=120+60+6=186$. (b) Mr Fon is in, so choose the other 4 members from the remaining 9 people: ${}^{9}C_{4}=\mathbf{126}$.

items_markdown: Multiply the numbers of ways for tasks done together ('and'), and add them for alternatives ('or').
Order matters: use ${}^{n}P_{r}=\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$. Order does not matter: use ${}^{n}C_{r}=\dfrac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$.
For a mixed group, choose from each set separately and multiply.
Repeated letters: divide $n!$ by the factorial of each repeat count.
For 'at least' questions, compare the direct cases with the complement; ${}^{n}C_{r}={}^{n}C_{n-r}$ shortens many calculations.
